module.title: Manufacturing and cross-industry solution patterns
module.summary: Frame plant-floor use cases from operational source to responsible human action: grain and metric contracts, event identity, units, timestamps and asset hierarchies; quality, traceability, engineering, maintenance, demand, scheduling and document patterns; transfer to other industries; and evidence-based verdicts.
objectives: Draw a use case's chain from operational source to responsible human action and write its metric contract at a declared grain.
Apply event identity, unit, timestamp and effective-dated asset hierarchy rules to quality, traceability, engineering, maintenance, demand, scheduling and document patterns.
Transfer a manufacturing pattern to retail, financial services or healthcare and write a use-case brief whose verdict may be 'not enough evidence yet'.

scenarios.title: Brief Cinderline's first plant-floor use case at Harwick
scenarios.context: Fictional Cinderline Components will fund one plant-floor use case at its Harwick plant this quarter. Three candidates: (1) supplier-lot traceability to narrow quality holds; (2) predicting porosity in die castings from process parameters so suspect castings get extra inspection; (3) an assistant answering technicians' questions from work instructions. Known facts: MES consumption events since 2024 at the lot × operation grain, 2.1% of them without a lot id; porosity labels come from X-ray, sampled 1 in 20 castings until March and 100% since, with 23 confirmed findings before March and 41 since; 30% of work instructions have no effective date in the document system; the Line 3 PLC clock drifts about 4 minutes a month and is reset at each shutdown.
scenarios.task: Write a use-case brief for the candidate you would take forward, and a short verdict for each of the other two. The brief contains a metric contract, the architecture from operational source to responsible human action, risks, evaluation criteria and an honest conclusion.
requirements: Give the chosen use case a metric contract with grain, numerator, denominator, aggregation, time basis, exclusions and owner.
Draw the chain from operational source through governed data and the decision to the named person who acts and records the outcome.
Name the identity, unit, timestamp, hierarchy and label risks that apply, each with a guard.
State evaluation criteria that could fail, and give every candidate a verdict; use 'not enough evidence yet' where the evidence cannot support a decision, saying what would change it.
scenarios.model:
### Chosen: supplier-lot traceability for quality holds
**Decision.** When a supplier or incoming inspection flags an input lot, the quality engineer holds only the produced lots and shipments it reached, instead of a week of output.

**Metric contract.** *Hold scope*: produced lots and shipments reached by a forward trace from the flagged lot. Grain lot × operation; time basis consumption time as a UTC instant, reported in site local days; exclusions none, with untraceable consumption reported beside the scope; owner quality engineering lead. Outcome metric: lots held per incident, and lots later found affected but outside the scope (target zero).

**Architecture.** MES consumption events → landing with source, event id and receive time → governed `genealogy_edges` keyed on (source system, event id, revision) → forward and backward trace job → hold list → quality engineer decides and records hold, release and later findings.

**Risks and guards.** 2.1% of events lack a lot id, mostly at the second casting hopper: report the gap on every trace and widen by time window there. Mixed hoppers: windowed edges marked as such. PLC drift: keep device and receive times; order by receive time within a shift where drift exceeds the window. Lineage shows how the tables were built; it is not the genealogy.

**Evaluation.** Replay the two holds of the last year: the trace must include every lot the manual hold found affected, with a smaller total scope. If either replay misses a lot, stop and fix capture first.

**Conclusion.** Pilot on Line 3 for one quarter.

### Porosity prediction: not enough evidence yet
Labels before March came from inspector-chosen X-rays, so they over-represent castings with visible defects; only the 41 findings since March come from 100% inspection. Review after two more quarters of full X-ray data, evaluated on a time-based split.

### Work-instruction assistant: fix data first
With 30% of instructions undated, the assistant could cite a superseded revision. Proceed after engineering restores effective dates; until then, a pilot limited to dated documents, refusing the rest, is acceptable.
scenarios.reasoning: The model picks the candidate whose decision owner, data and outcome evidence already exist, gives it a contract and guards drawn from identity, clock and completeness risks, and writes evaluation criteria that can fail. It refuses to call a biased label set evidence and treats undated documents as a data fix, so each verdict follows from named evidence rather than from enthusiasm.

rubric.weak: A metric named without grain, denominator or owner.
rubric.partial: Grain and ratio stated, but time basis, exclusions or owner missing.
rubric.strong: Grain, numerator, denominator, aggregation, time basis, exclusions and owner all stated, with an outcome metric that could show harm.

rubric.criterion: Chain from source to responsible action
rubric.weak: A platform diagram ending in a dashboard.
rubric.partial: Sources and tables drawn, but no named person or outcome record.
rubric.strong: Every link named, with event identity at the governed layer and the engineer's decision and outcome recorded.

rubric.partial: Specific risks named without guards, or lineage treated as genealogy.
rubric.strong: Missing lot ids, mixing, clock drift and label bias each named with a guard and a reported measure.

rubric.weak: All three candidates approved, or criteria that cannot fail.
rubric.partial: Criteria stated but a biased label set treated as sufficient.
rubric.strong: Failable criteria, one pilot, 'not enough evidence yet' for porosity with the evidence and review date that would change it, and a data fix named for the assistant.

disclosures.question: Were the X-ray samples before March random?
disclosures.response: No. Until March the inspector chose which castings to X-ray, usually after seeing a surface defect. Since March every casting is X-rayed.

disclosures.question: Why do 2.1% of consumption events lack a lot id?
disclosures.response: Operators scan the lot label at the hopper; when a label is damaged they key UNKNOWN. Most gaps are at the second hopper of the casting cell.

disclosures.question: When will the work instructions have effective dates?
disclosures.response: Engineering says the migrated documents will be re-dated within about two months; the document owners have agreed to do it.

concepts.definition: The path from an operational source through governed data and a decision to a named person who acts and records the outcome.
A written definition of a metric's grain, numerator, denominator, aggregation, time basis, exclusions and owner.
The fields that name one real occurrence, such as source system, record id and revision.
A dated parent-child structure placing each asset under the one that contains it, from site to sensor.
Units passing their first inspection without rework, divided by units entering the operation.
Recorded consumption links between input lots, produced lots, serials and shipments, walked forward or backward.
The recorded maintenance outcome, within a horizon after the prediction time, that a model learns to predict.
Demand hidden by a stock-out, so recorded shipments for that period are only a lower bound.
A schedule that respects capacity, changeovers, material availability and maintenance windows before it is judged on lateness.
The status and effective date of one version of a controlled document, deciding which text may be cited.
Re-deriving identity, grain, hierarchy, clock and responsible person when a pattern moves to another industry.
A use-case conclusion naming the evidence that supports it or the evidence that would change it.
